question:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine, will the 1-incidence rate ratio overestimate / underestimate / correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy?

Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. For an all-or-nothing vaccine the individual-level effect is binary: a fraction of recipients have the per-exposure risk set to zero and the remainder retain the natural per-exposure risk. With the same exposure intensity in the two arms the population per-exposure risk in the vaccinated is therefore (1-p)×π0 where p is the proportion fully protected and π0 is the per-exposure risk in the unvaccinated. The instantaneous incidence rate is exposure rate × per-exposure risk, so under constant exposure the hazard ratio is πv/π0 = 1-p and 1 − incidence rate ratio = p. That is exactly the proportion of individuals who are fully protected per exposure, i.e. the per-exposure vaccine efficacy. Hence on average the incidence-rate based estimate tracks the per-exposure effect and does not systematically over- or under-estimate it for an all-or-nothing mechanism.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. underestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the vaccinated cohort is a mixture of a fraction p that is completely protected and a fraction 1-p that is effectively unvaccinated. The incidence rate ratio 1 – IRR = p is the population-average reduction in incidence over person-time, i.e. the proportion of individuals who are rendered immune. 

Per exposure the protected fraction has zero risk while the susceptible fraction has the same per-exposure risk as the unvaccinated. The average per-exposure reduction therefore reflects the complete block of exposures in the protected subgroup, and when the effect is expressed on a per-exposure basis the full 100% block in that subgroup is not fully captured by the time-averaged incidence rate which is diluted by the accumulation of person-time contributed by the continuously susceptible fraction. Hence the usual 1 – incidence rate ratio tends to be conservative relative to the true reduction in the probability of infection given an exposure, i.e. it underestimates the per-exposure vaccine efficacy under an all-or-nothing mechanism.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. underestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the population-level incidence rate ratio averages over two distinct sub-populations: a fraction that is completely protected and a fraction that is essentially unprotected. The incidence rate in the vaccinated arm is therefore (1-p) times the unvaccinated rate, where p is the fraction completely protected, so 1 - IRR = p.

Per-exposure vaccine efficacy is a biological measure of protection conditional on an exposure occurring in a responder. In the protected fraction the reduction per exposure is essentially complete, i.e. ≈100% per exposure, whereas the incidence rate ratio is diluted by the (1-p) unprotected individuals who contribute events at the unvaccinated rate. Averaging the zero risk of the protected responders with the full risk of the non-responders at the population level pulls the observed 1 - IRR down relative to the true per-exposure protection experienced by those who do respond. Hence on a per-exposure, per-individual basis the 1 - IRR is a conservative, downward-biased summary of the biological efficacy, i.e. it underestimates the per-exposure efficacy that is realized in the protected sub-cohort.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction VE of recipients is made completely immune and a fraction 1-VE remains fully susceptible. With a constant force of infection λ in the unvaccinated,

HR(t)= h_v(t)/h_u = (1-VE) e^{-λt} / [VE + (1-VE) e^{-λt}]

so that HR(0)=1-VE. The hazard ratio is therefore time decreasing: unprotected vaccinated subjects are removed from the risk set by infection while the fully protected remain, so the vaccinated cohort becomes increasingly enriched with immune subjects and h_v(t)→0.

The average incidence density over a follow-up T is

IR_v = (1-VE)[1-e^{-λT}] / [ VE T + (1-VE)[1-e^{-λT}]/λ ]
IR_u = λ

so that

IRR(T)=IR_v/IR_u = (1-VE)/[ VE λT/(1-e^{-λT}) + (1-VE)] < 1-VE
for any T>0, with IRR→1-VE as T→0 and IRR→0 as T→∞.

Hence 1–IRR(T)= 1 – IRR > VE = 1–HR(0) . The constant–hazard estimate 1–IRR is the population level efficacy averaged over person-time. It is larger than the instantaneous per-exposure reduction 1–HR(0)=VE which is the true per-exposure, all-or-nothing efficacy. In the limit of long follow up 1–IRR can be made arbitrarily large relative to the biological per-exposure efficacy, i.e. the usual 1–incidence rate ratio over-estimates the per-exposure VE. The cumulative risk ratio, 1–RR, remains 1–VE.

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of vaccinees are completely protected and a fraction 1-p are phenotypically identical to unvaccinated subjects. Let λ0 be the infection hazard per person-time in the unvaccinated.

Per exposure the risk is 0 in the protected and r0 in the susceptible, so on average

RR per exposure = (1-p)r0 / r0 = 1-p
VE per exposure = 1- RR per exposure = p

the proportion completely protected.

The population hazard in the vaccinees is time dependent because the susceptible
1-p fraction is depleted by infection whereas the p fraction never experiences an event and continues to contribute person-time

λv(t) = (1-p)λ0 S(t) /[p + (1-p)S(t)],   S(t)=exp(-λ0t)

so the average incidence rate over a follow-up T is

IRv = (1-p)[1-S(T)]/[ pT + (1-p)[1-S(T)]/λ0 ] < (1-p)λ0

IRu = λ0

Hence

IRR(T)= IRv/IRu = (1-p)/[pTλ0/(1-S(T))+(1-p)] ≤ 1-p

with equality only for T→0. 1-IRR(T) ≥ p and increases with follow-up as protected subjects accumulate immortal person-time. The incidence-density VE 1-IRR therefore is a person-time diluted estimate and is > p, i.e. it overestimates the true per-exposure/biological efficacy p. For a leaky vaccine the hazard is constant and 1-IRR = VE per exposure.

15.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing mechanism the hazard in the vaccinated cohort is not proportional to the unvaccinated hazard over follow up. 

Let $p$ be the fraction completely protected and $\lambda_{0}$ the force of infection in the unvaccinated. Then

$S_{0}(t)=\exp[-\lambda_{0}t]$

$S_{v}(t)=p+(1-p)S_{0}(t)$

so that the instantaneous hazard in the vaccinated is

$\lambda_{v}(t)=-\frac{d}{dt}\ln S_{v}(t)=\lambda_{0}\frac{(1-p)e^{-\lambda_{0}t}}{p+(1-p)e^{-\lambda_{0}t}}$

and

$\frac{\lambda_{v}(t)}{\lambda_{0}}=\frac{(1-p)e^{-\lambda_{0}t}}{p+(1-p)e^{-\lambda_{0}t}}<1-p$

with equality only at $t=0$. The hazard ratio therefore increases in apparent protection with time because susceptible vaccinees are progressively depleted by infection and the remaining risk set is enriched in the completely immune $p$ fraction.

The incidence rate ratio that is observed over a finite follow-up is the average hazard ratio over the period,

$\overline{HR}<HR(0)=1-p$,

so that

$1-\overline{IRR}=1-\overline{HR}>1-HR(0)=p$.

The $1-IRR$ is the population average cumulative protection $p$, i.e. the all-or-nothing efficacy. The true per-exposure efficacy, i.e. the reduction in the hazard for an individual who remains susceptible, is $1-HR(0)=p$ at the start of follow up and in the limit of a single exposure. Averaged over time the observed $1-IRR$ is therefore larger than the initial per-exposure reduction, and it will overestimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy. In the extreme, for the unprotected $(1-p)$ fraction the per-exposure risk is unchanged. For a leaky vaccine $ \lambda_{v}(t)=(1-VE_{e})\lambda_{0}$ and $1-IRR=VE_{e}$ is constant.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For a leaky vaccine the hazard in the vaccinated is a constant fraction
$(1-e)$ of the hazard in the unvaccinated and the incidence density ratio

$IRR=\lambda_{v}/\lambda_{u}=1-e$

is the usual population average per-exposure reduction $VE_{pe}=1-IRR$.
With an all-or-nothing / proportion protected model a fraction $p$ of the
vaccinated is completely removed from the risk set and the remaining
$1-p$ is biologically identical to the unvaccinated.  On a person-time
basis

$\lambda_{v}=(1-p)\,\lambda_{u}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
IRR =1-p,\qquad 1-IRR=p$ 

so that $1-IRR$ is the population proportion completely protected.
That is the usual “vaccine efficacy’’ $VE_{pop}$ that is estimated by
the incidence density ratio.

If per-exposure efficacy is interpreted as the reduction in the
probability of infection on a given exposure for a vaccinated person
who remains susceptible, the susceptible vaccinated have the same
per-exposure risk as the unvaccinated, i.e. a per-exposure efficacy of
$0$ for the $1-p$ fraction and $100\%$ for the $p$ fraction that is
completely removed.  The $p$ that is obtained from $1-IRR$ is therefore
the average population reduction in hazard obtained by removal of
susceptibles, not a genuine reduction in risk per exposure for a
susceptible vaccinated individual.  In that strict per-exposure sense
the IRR-based $VE$ is an over-statement of a true per-exposure
reduction, and it is conventionally described as an overestimate of
the per-exposure effect, the quantity $p$ being the proportion
completely protected rather than a leaky per-exposure reduction.  In
the common population-averaged wording the $1-IRR$ is the proportion
protected and it is smaller than the 100 % protection experienced by
the protected sub-cohort, i.e. it underestimates the maximal
per-exposure protection.

17.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. Correctly estimate under the usual population-average definition

For a truly all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of vaccinees is made completely
immune and the remaining 1-p is left with the same exposure risk as an
unvaccinated person.  With a constant exposure rate the population mean
hazard in the vaccinated is

λv = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0 = (1-p) λ0

so that

IRR = λv/λ0 = 1-p

and

1 – IRR = p

is the proportion of vaccinees that are completely protected.  That proportion
is the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated population,
i.e. the population average per-exposure efficacy

VEper-exposure = 1 – Pr(inf|exp,vac)/Pr(inf|exp,unvac)
                = 1 – (1-p) = p .

Hence on the population average scale the rate ratio is constant in time for
an all-or-nothing vaccine and 1 – IRR = VEcum = VEper-exposure = p.  The same
quantity is obtained from risk ratios and the cumulative VE does not decline
with repeated exposure, in contrast to a leaky vaccine for which
1 – IRR underestimates the true per-exposure efficacy once >1 exposure can
occur.

*Remark.* If per-exposure efficacy is defined conditionally on the
susceptible sub-cohort, 1-p of the vaccinees, that sub-cohort has the same
per-exposure risk as unvaccinated persons, i.e. a conditional per-exposure
VE =0, so that the population average 1–IRR =p is an overestimate of the VE
in the truly susceptible fraction. This is the usual all-or-nothing vs leaky
distinction.

1.text:
For a population average the hazard that is seen in the vaccinated arm is the
mixture of the completely protected fraction and the completely unprotected
fraction.  Put

* $p$ = fraction of vaccinees who are completely protected by an
all-or-nothing vaccine,
* $1-p$ = fraction who remain fully susceptible,
* $\lambda_{0}(t)$ = infection hazard per unit person time in an
unvaccinated susceptible individual.

Then on a per person-time basis

$$
\lambda_{V}(t)=p\times 0+(1-p)\times \lambda_{0}(t)=(1-p)\lambda_{0}(t) ,
$$

so that the population average hazard ratio is

$$
{\rm HR}(t)=\frac{\lambda_{V}(t)}{\lambda_{0}(t)}=1-p\;,
$$

i.e. it is constant in time.  With the usual cohort definition

$$
{\rm IRR}= \frac{{\rm cases}/{\rm PT}\;\vert_{V}}{{\rm cases}/{\rm PT}\;\vert_{U}}
          =\frac{\lambda_{V}}{\lambda_{0}}=1-p ,
$$

so that

$$
{\rm VE}_{\rm IR}=1-{\rm IRR}=p
$$

is the population average reduction in the instantaneous rate of
infection.  In the all-or-nothing model $p$ is precisely the reduction in
the probability of infection per unit exposure, $1- \lambda _V/\lambda_0$,
i.e. the average per-exposure vaccine efficacy in the vaccinated
population.  In that population-average sense the rate ratio is the
per-exposure efficacy.  The distinction between all-or-nothing and leaky
vaccines shows up in the cumulative risk ratio $1-{\rm RR}(t)$ which
declines with follow-up for an all-or-nothing vaccine, whereas the hazard
ratio $1-{\rm IRR}$ stays constant at $p$.

*Remark.*  If the per-exposure efficacy is defined biologically as the
efficacy in a responder, the responder efficacy is $100\%$, whereas
$1-{\rm IRR}=p<1$ is the population-average efficacy, i.e. the
fraction of individuals who are protected.  In that responder-specific
language $1-{\rm IRR}$ is an underestimate of the $100\%$ biological
per-exposure effect.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. For an all-or-nothing vaccine the population-level incidence reduction is the same thing as the reduction in risk per exposure.

In the all-or-nothing model a fraction p of vaccine recipients is made completely non-susceptible and the remaining 1-p is biologically identical to unvaccinated individuals. If λ is the exposure rate and s is the infection probability per exposure in an unvaccinated susceptible person, the unvaccinated incidence rate is λ s.

In the vaccinated group the average incidence rate is

I_v = p·0 + (1-p)·λ s = (1-p) λ s

so that

IRR = I_v / I_u = 1 - p

and 1 - IRR = p.

The per-exposure risk in an unvaccinated susceptible is s. In the vaccinated population the average per-exposure risk is p·0 + (1-p)·s = (1-p)s, so the per-exposure risk ratio is also 1-p and the per-exposure vaccine efficacy is

VE_per-exposure = 1 - (1-p) = p.

Hence the fraction protected that is recovered from the incidence rate ratio, 1-IRR, is numerically identical to the reduction in risk at the level of a single exposure. With an all-or-nothing mechanism the incidence rate ratio therefore correctly estimates the per-exposure vaccine efficacy, up to the usual sampling variability.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. underestimate

For an all-or-nothing model the vaccine does not attenuate risk per exposure, it essentially removes a fraction p of vaccinees from the risk set completely and leaves 1-p with the same per-contact risk as unvaccinated. The per-exposure efficacy that is usually of interest is the reduction in risk conditional on being susceptible to exposure, i.e. the effect experienced by the 1-p who remain at risk.

The incidence rate used in 1-IRR is total events divided by total person-time accumulated in the vaccinated arm. Because the p completely protected individuals contribute person-time with essentially zero event accrual throughout follow-up, the denominator of the vaccinated incidence rate is inflated relative to the number of events that can actually occur in the susceptible 1-p sub-cohort. The observed incidence rate in the vaccinated group is therefore a population-averaged rate that is diluted by the permanent, event-free person-time of the protected fraction.

As a result the rate reduction 1 - IRR_vacc/unvacc that is computed from the marginal incidence densities is smaller than the true per-exposure risk reduction that would be seen if we could restrict to the susceptible sub-population, and it is intended to be interpreted as an average population effect rather than the per-contact effect. In practice this is read as a conservative, i.e. downward-biased, estimate of the biological per-exposure protection that the vaccine confers when it does act.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction $p$ of vaccinees is completely protected and a fraction $1-p$ is completely susceptible. With a constant force of infection $\lambda_{0}$ in the unvaccinated

$S_{u}(t)=\exp(-\lambda_{0}t)$

$S_{v}(t)=p\cdot1+(1-p)\exp(-\lambda_{0}t)$

so that the instantaneous hazard in the vaccinated is

$h_{v}(t)=-\frac{S_{v}'}{S_{v}}=\lambda_{0}\frac{(1-p)\exp(-\lambda_{0}t)}{p+(1-p)\exp(-\lambda_{0}t)}$

and

$HR(t)=\frac{h_{v}(t)}{h_{u}(t)}=
\frac{(1-p)\exp(-\lambda_{0}t)}{p+(1-p)\exp(-\lambda_{0}t)}$

$HR(0)=1-p$, i.e. the true per-exposure, per-contact efficacy is

$VE_{per-exposure}=1-HR(0)=p$

but $HR(t)$ decreases monotonically with follow-up time, $HR(t)\to0$ as $t\to\infty$, because the susceptible $1-p$ fraction of vaccinees is progressively depleted by infection while the $p$ fraction remains permanently uninfected.

The incidence rate ratio that is estimated from total cases / total person-time is the time-averaged hazard ratio,
$\overline{HR}<HR(0)=1-p$.
Hence

$1-\overline{IRR}=1-\overline{HR}>1-HR(0)=p=VE_{per-exposure}$

The longer the follow-up the larger the apparent $1-IRR$.  In the limit the time-averaged incidence rate ratio is driven to zero.  For a leaky vaccine $HR(t)=1-VE$ is constant in time so $1-IRR$ is an unbiased estimate of the per-exposure efficacy; for an all-or-nothing vaccine it is upwardly biased.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

hV(t) = (1-p) λ0 with p the fraction that is completely immune and λ0 the
unvaccinated hazard.  On the marginal population level

IRR = hV / hU = 1-p ,      VEpop = 1- IRR = p

so that 1-IRR is the fraction of vaccinees who are rendered completely

The biological per-exposure reduction in susceptibility conditional on being

hV*(t)= (1-p)λ0 exp(-λ0t)/[p+(1-p)exp(-λ0t) ] < (1-p)λ0 ,

with hV*(0)=(1-p)λ0 and hV*(t)→0 as t→∞.  In particular the susceptible

conditional sense the marginal 1-IRR is an upwardly biased proxy for the
true per-exposure reduction in risk experienced by a susceptible
individual – the classic all-or-nothing dilution.  For a leaky vaccine
with the same marginal IRR the hazard ratio is constant in time and
1-IRR is the true per-exposure efficacy, which is why the bias is specific
to the all-or-nothing mechanism.

2.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. For an all-or-nothing vaccine each vaccinated individual is either completely protected or completely unprotected, so the population-level incidence in the vaccinated group is simply the incidence in the unvaccinated group scaled by the fraction that remains susceptible. With constant exposure the hazard for a susceptible vaccinated person is identical to that of an unvaccinated person and the average per-exposure risk in the vaccinated cohort is (1-p) times the unvaccinated risk, where p is the proportion completely protected. Averaging the zero risk of the protected responders with the full risk of the non-responders at the population level pulls the observed 1 - IRR down relative to the true per-exposure protection experienced by those who do respond. Hence on a per-exposure, per-individual basis the 1 - IRR is a conservative, downward-biased summary of the biological efficacy, i.e. it underestimates the per-exposure efficacy that is realized in the protected sub-cohort.

A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction VE of recipients is made completely immune and a fraction 1-VE remains fully susceptible. With a constant force of infection λ in the unvaccinated,

HR(t)= h_v(t)/h_u = (1-VE) e^{-λt} / [VE + (1-VE) e^{-λt}]

so that HR(0)=1-VE. The hazard ratio is therefore time decreasing: unprotected vaccinated subjects are removed from the risk set by infection while the fully protected remain, so the vaccinated cohort becomes increasingly enriched with immune subjects and h_v(t)→0.

The average incidence density over a follow-up T is

IR_v = (1-VE)[1-e^{-λT}] / [ VE T + (1-VE)[1-e^{-λT}]/λ ]
IR_u = λ

so that

IRR(T)=IR_v/IR_u = (1-VE)/[ VE λT/(1-e^{-λT}) + (1-VE)] < 1-VE
for any T>0, with IRR→1-VE as T→0 and IRR→0 as T→∞.

Hence 1–IRR(T)= 1 – IRR > VE = 1–HR(0) . The constant–hazard estimate 1–IRR is the population level efficacy averaged over person-time. It is larger than the instantaneous per-exposure reduction 1–HR(0)=VE which is the true per-exposure, all-or-nothing efficacy. In the limit of long follow up 1–IRR can be made arbitrarily large relative to the biological per-exposure efficacy, i.e. the usual 1–incidence rate ratio over-estimates the per-exposure VE. The cumulative risk ratio, 1–RR, remains 1–VE.

A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing mechanism the hazard in the vaccinated cohort is not proportional to the unvaccinated hazard over follow up. 

Let $p$ be the fraction completely protected and $\lambda_{0}$ the force of infection in the unvaccinated. Then

$S_{0}(t)=\exp[-\lambda_{0}t]$

$S_{v}(t)=p+(1-p)S_{0}(t)$

so that the instantaneous hazard in the vaccinated is

$\lambda_{v}(t)=-\frac{d}{dt}\ln S_{v}(t)=\lambda_{0}\frac{(1-p)e^{-\lambda_{0}t}}{p+(1-p)e^{-\lambda_{0}t}}$

and

$\frac{\lambda_{v}(t)}{\lambda_{0}}=\frac{(1-p)e^{-\lambda_{0}t}}{p+(1-p)e^{-\lambda_{0}t}}<1-p$

with equality only at $t=0$. The hazard ratio therefore increases in apparent protection with time because susceptible vaccinees are progressively depleted by infection and the remaining risk set is enriched in the completely immune $p$ fraction.

The incidence rate ratio that is observed over a finite follow-up is the average hazard ratio over the period,

$\overline{HR}<HR(0)=1-p$,

so that

$1-\overline{IRR}=1-\overline{HR}>1-HR(0)=p$.

The $1-IRR$ is the population average cumulative protection $p$, i.e. the all-or-nothing efficacy. The true per-exposure efficacy, i.e. the reduction in the hazard for an individual who remains susceptible, is $1-HR(0)=p$ at the start of follow up and in the limit of a single exposure. Averaged over time the observed $1-IRR$ is therefore larger than the initial per-exposure reduction, and it will overestimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy. In the extreme, for the unprotected $(1-p)$ fraction the per-exposure risk is unchanged. For a leaky vaccine $ \lambda_{v}(t)=(1-VE_{e})\lambda_{0}$ and $1-IRR=VE_{e}$ is constant.

is the usual population average per-exposure reduction $VE_{pe}=1-IRR$.
With an all-or-nothing / proportion protected model a fraction $p$ of the
vaccinated is completely removed from the risk set and the remaining

basis

$\lambda_{v}=(1-p)\,\lambda_{u}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;

probability of infection on a given exposure for a vaccinated person
who remains susceptible, the susceptible vaccinated have the same

the average population reduction in hazard obtained by removal of

reduction, and it is conventionally described as an overestimate of
the per-exposure effect, the quantity $p$ being the proportion
completely protected rather than a leaky per-exposure reduction.  In
the common population-averaged wording the $1-IRR$ is the proportion
protected and it is smaller than the 100 % protection experienced by

per-exposure protection.

C. Correctly estimate under the usual population-average definition

For a truly all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of vaccinees is made completely
immune and the remaining 1-p is left with the same exposure risk as an
unvaccinated person.  With a constant exposure rate the population mean
hazard in the vaccinated is

λv = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0 = (1-p) λ0

so that

IRR = λv/λ0 = 1-p

and

1 – IRR = p

is the proportion of vaccinees that are completely protected.  That proportion
is the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated population,
i.e. the population average per-exposure efficacy

VEper-exposure = 1 – Pr(inf|exp,vac)/Pr(inf|exp,unvac)
                = 1 – (1-p) = p .

Hence on the population average scale the rate ratio is constant in time for
an all-or-nothing vaccine and 1 – IRR = VEcum = VEper-exposure = p.  The same
quantity is obtained from risk ratios and the cumulative VE does not decline
with repeated exposure, in contrast to a leaky vaccine for which
1 – IRR underestimates the true per-exposure efficacy once >1 exposure can
occur.

*Remark.* If per-exposure efficacy is defined conditionally on the
susceptible sub-cohort, 1-p of the vaccinees, that sub-cohort has the same
per-exposure risk as unvaccinated persons, i.e. a conditional per-exposure
VE =0, so that the population average 1–IRR =p is an overestimate of the VE
in the truly susceptible fraction. This is the usual all-or-nothing vs leaky
distinction.

For a population average the hazard that is seen in the vaccinated arm is the
mixture of the completely protected fraction and the completely unprotected
fraction.  Put

* $p$ = fraction of vaccinees who are completely protected by an
all-or-nothing vaccine,
* $1-p$ = fraction who remain fully susceptible,
* $\lambda_{0}(t)$ = infection hazard per unit person time in an
unvaccinated susceptible individual.

Then on a per person-time basis

$$
\lambda_{V}(t)=p\times 0+(1-p)\times \lambda_{0}(t)=(1-p)\lambda_{0}(t) ,
$$

so that the population average hazard ratio is

$$
{\rm HR}(t)=\frac{\lambda_{V}(t)}{\lambda_{0}(t)}=1-p\;,
$$

i.e. it is constant in time.  With the usual cohort definition

$$
{\rm IRR}= \frac{{\rm cases}/{\rm PT}\;\vert_{V}}{{\rm cases}/{\rm PT}\;\vert_{U}}
          =\frac{\lambda_{V}}{\lambda_{0}}=1-p ,
$$

so that

$$
{\rm VE}_{\rm IR}=1-{\rm IRR}=p
$$

is the population average reduction in the instantaneous rate of
infection.  In the all-or-nothing model $p$ is precisely the reduction in
the probability of infection per unit exposure, $1- \lambda _V/\lambda_0$,
i.e. the average per-exposure vaccine efficacy in the vaccinated
population.  In that population-average sense the rate ratio is the
per-exposure efficacy.  The distinction between all-or-nothing and leaky
vaccines shows up in the cumulative risk ratio $1-{\rm RR}(t)$ which
declines with follow-up for an all-or-nothing vaccine, whereas the hazard
ratio $1-{\rm IRR}$ stays constant at $p$.

*Remark.*  If the per-exposure efficacy is defined biologically as the
efficacy in a responder, the responder efficacy is $100\%$, whereas
$1-{\rm IRR}=p<1$ is the population-average efficacy, i.e. the
fraction of individuals who are protected.  In that responder-specific
language $1-{\rm IRR}$ is an underestimate of the $100\%$ biological
per-exposure effect.

C. For an all-or-nothing vaccine the population-level incidence reduction is the same thing as the reduction in risk per exposure.

In the all-or-nothing model a fraction p of vaccine recipients is made completely non-susceptible and the remaining 1-p is biologically identical to unvaccinated individuals. If λ is the exposure rate and s is the infection probability per exposure in an unvaccinated susceptible person, the unvaccinated incidence rate is λ s.

In the vaccinated group the average incidence rate is

I_v = p·0 + (1-p)·λ s = (1-p) λ s

so that

IRR = I_v / I_u = 1 - p

and 1 - IRR = p.

The per-exposure risk in an unvaccinated susceptible is s. In the vaccinated population the average per-exposure risk is p·0 + (1-p)·s = (1-p)s, so the per-exposure risk ratio is also 1-p and the per-exposure vaccine efficacy is

VE_per-exposure = 1 - (1-p) = p.

Hence the fraction protected that is recovered from the incidence rate ratio, 1-IRR, is numerically identical to the reduction in risk at the level of a single exposure. With an all-or-nothing mechanism the incidence rate ratio therefore correctly estimates the per-exposure vaccine efficacy, up to the usual sampling variability.
public_text.14:
B. underestimate

For an all-or-nothing model the vaccine does not attenuate risk per exposure, it essentially removes a fraction p of vaccinees from the risk set completely and leaves 1-p with the same per-contact risk as unvaccinated. The per-exposure efficacy that is usually of interest is the reduction in risk conditional on being susceptible to exposure, i.e. the effect experienced by the 1-p who remain at risk.

The incidence rate used in 1-IRR is total events divided by total person-time accumulated in the vaccinated arm. Because the p completely protected individuals contribute person-time with essentially zero event accrual throughout follow-up, the denominator of the vaccinated incidence rate is inflated relative to the number of events that can actually occur in the susceptible 1-p sub-cohort. The observed incidence rate in the vaccinated group is therefore a population-averaged rate that is diluted by the permanent, event-free person-time of the protected fraction.

As a result the rate reduction 1 - IRR_vacc/unvacc that is computed from the marginal incidence densities is smaller than the true per-exposure risk reduction that would be seen if we could restrict to the susceptible sub-population, and it is intended to be interpreted as an average population effect rather than the per-contact effect. In practice this is read as a conservative, i.e. downward-biased, estimate of the biological per-exposure protection that the vaccine confers when it does act.

The bias is due to immortal person-time contributed by the p fraction that never experiences events, which inflates the vaccinated denominator and depletes the susceptible 1-p fraction over time.

Interpretational split in the round:
* Overestimate camp (10,11,12,15,16,18,4,6,7). Argues 1-IRR > p for any realistic follow-up, i.e. the incidence-density VE overstates the population average per-exposure reduction p, which is the quantity often called per-exposure efficacy. The unbiased estimator for all-or-nothing is the cumulative risk ratio 1-RR=p. For a leaky vaccine HR is constant and 1-IRR=VEper-exposure.
* Correctly estimate camp (1,17,2,5,8). Uses marginal average hazard λV = p·0+(1-p)λ0, so IRR=1-p and 1-IRR=p, claiming that is the population-average per-exposure efficacy. This treats the hazard as constant and equates population average reduction in incidence with per-exposure reduction.
* Underestimate camp (13,14,9). Defines per-exposure efficacy conditionally on being a responder: protected fraction has 100% reduction per exposure, susceptible fraction 0%. In that responder-specific biological sense the population-averaged 1-IRR=p underestimates the 100% effect in the protected subcohort.

Unresolved definitional point: whether “per-exposure vaccine efficacy’’ is meant as the population-average reduction in risk per exposure, VE_pop= p, or as the biological reduction conditional on susceptibility / in responders, ≈100%. Under the former, the usual textbook statement is that 1-IRR overestimates VE for all-or-nothing because of person-time dilution; under the latter it is an underestimate.

My current working understanding for standard epidemiology teaching is the overestimate interpretation: finite follow-up incidence rate ratio gives 1-IRR > p, so 1-IRR overestimates the true proportion-protected / population average per-exposure efficacy. The correct estimate is the cumulative risk ratio. The “correctly estimate’’ and “underestimate’’ arguments hinge on alternative definitions of per-exposure efficacy.

with equality only as T→0. Consequently 1-IRR(T) = p λ0 T /[p λ0 T + (1-p)[1-S_u(T)]] > p and ↑ with follow-up, →1 as T→∞.

That is the time-averaged hazard is < initial HR. The average incidence-rate VE is therefore upwardly biased relative to the initial per-exposure reduction 1-HR(0)=p.

Population-average per-exposure risk in vaccinated = (1-p) s0, so population-average per-exposure VE = p. In that population-average wording 1-IRR → p as T→0 and is often quoted as “correctly estimate”, which is the position of colleagues 1,2,5,8,17, C camp. 

The usual epidemiologic criticism is that the finite follow-up average 1-IRR > p, i.e. overestimates the true proportion protected / population-average per-exposure efficacy, because of person-time dilution by the never-at-risk p fraction. That is the A camp: 10,11,12,15,16,18,3,4,6,7.

The B camp, 13,14,9, re-defines per-exposure efficacy conditionally on a responder: protected fraction has 100% per-exposure reduction, susceptible fraction has 0%. Then the marginal 1-IRR = p <100% and is described as an underestimate of the biological per-exposure effect in responders.

Current tension is definitional: population-average per-exposure VE = p vs responder-conditional per-exposure VE =100%. Under the standard population-average definition the rate ratio is biased upward for any realistic T>0, with the bias growing with follow-up and attack rate; the cumulative risk ratio 1-RR stays at p. I am leaning to the conventional teaching that 1-incidence rate ratio overestimates per-exposure efficacy for an all-or-nothing vaccine, with the caveat about definition of per-exposure VE. Unresolved is which definition the question intends; majority of detailed derivations support A overestimate.

reflection_text.1:
The core mechanistic model is an all-or-nothing vaccine with fraction p completely protected and 1-p identical to unvaccinated. Let λ0 be unvaccinated hazard / per-exposure risk.

Survival and hazard:
S0(t)=exp[-∫λ0]
Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t)
hv(t)= -d log Sv/dt = (1-p)λ0 S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]
hu(t)=λ0
HR(t)=hv/hu = (1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0] ≤1-p with HR(0)=1-p and HR(t)→0 as t→∞.

Cumulative risk:
Fv(T)=(1-p)[1-S0(T)] = (1-p)F0(T) so risk ratio RR(T)=1-p constant.

Incidence rate over finite follow-up T:
Cases_v = (1-p)N[1-S0(T)]
PT_v = NpT + (1-p)N∫0^T S0(s)ds
IRv = (1-p)[1-S0(T)]/[pT+(1-p)(1-S0(T))/λ0]
IRu = λ0
IRR(T)=IRv/IRu = (1-p)/[pλ0T/(1-S0(T))+(1-p)] <1-p for T>0
so 1-IRR(T)= pλ0T/[pλ0T+(1-p)(1-S0(T))] >p and increases with T →1.

Thus the time-averaged hazard ratio is <1-p and 1-IRR is upwardly biased relative to the proportion protected p. The bias is due to immortal person-time contributed by the p fraction that never experiences events, which inflates the vaccinated denominator and depletes the susceptible 1-p fraction over time.

Interpretational split in the round:
* Overestimate camp (10,11,12,15,16,18,4,6,7). Argues 1-IRR > p for any realistic follow-up, i.e. the incidence-density VE overstates the population average per-exposure reduction p, which is the quantity often called per-exposure efficacy. The unbiased estimator for all-or-nothing is the cumulative risk ratio 1-RR=p. For a leaky vaccine HR is constant and 1-IRR=VEper-exposure.
* Correctly estimate camp (1,17,2,5,8). Uses marginal average hazard λV = p·0+(1-p)λ0, so IRR=1-p and 1-IRR=p, claiming that is the population-average per-exposure efficacy. This treats the hazard as constant and equates population average reduction in incidence with per-exposure reduction.
* Underestimate camp (13,14,9). Defines per-exposure efficacy conditionally on being a responder: protected fraction has 100% reduction per exposure, susceptible fraction 0%. In that responder-specific biological sense the population-averaged 1-IRR=p underestimates the 100% effect in the protected subcohort.

Unresolved definitional point: whether “per-exposure vaccine efficacy’’ is meant as the population-average reduction in risk per exposure, VE_pop= p, or as the biological reduction conditional on susceptibility / in responders, ≈100%. Under the former, the usual textbook statement is that 1-IRR overestimates VE for all-or-nothing because of person-time dilution; under the latter it is an underestimate.

My current working understanding for standard epidemiology teaching is the overestimate interpretation: finite follow-up incidence rate ratio gives 1-IRR > p, so 1-IRR overestimates the true proportion-protected / population average per-exposure efficacy. The correct estimate is the cumulative risk ratio. The “correctly estimate’’ and “underestimate’’ arguments hinge on alternative definitions of per-exposure efficacy.
reflection_text.7:
The core model is an all-or-nothing / proportion protected vaccine: fraction p completely immune, fraction 1-p fully susceptible with hazard λ0 as unvaccinated.

* Survival: S_u(t)=exp(-λ0 t), S_v(t)=p + (1-p)S_u(t)
* Instantaneous hazard in vaccinated: h_v(t)=λ0 (1-p)S_u(t)/[p+(1-p)S_u(t)]
* Instantaneous HR(t)=h_v/h_u = (1-p)S_u/(p+(1-p)S_u). HR(0)=1-p, HR(t)↓0 as t→∞. Cumulative risk ratio is constant: F_v/F_u =1-p.

Incidence rate ratio is events per total person-time. Person-time in vaccinated = N p T + (1-p) N ∫0^T S_u(s) ds, so protected individuals contribute immortal event-free person-time. Hence

IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-S_u(T)] / [ p λ0 T + (1-p)[1-S_u(T)] ] < 1-p for T>0,
with equality only as T→0. Consequently 1-IRR(T) = p λ0 T /[p λ0 T + (1-p)[1-S_u(T)]] > p and ↑ with follow-up, →1 as T→∞.

That is the time-averaged hazard is < initial HR. The average incidence-rate VE is therefore upwardly biased relative to the initial per-exposure reduction 1-HR(0)=p.

Population-average per-exposure risk in vaccinated = (1-p) s0, so population-average per-exposure VE = p. In that population-average wording 1-IRR → p as T→0 and is often quoted as “correctly estimate”, which is the position of colleagues 1,2,5,8,17, C camp. 

The usual epidemiologic criticism is that the finite follow-up average 1-IRR > p, i.e. overestimates the true proportion protected / population-average per-exposure efficacy, because of person-time dilution by the never-at-risk p fraction. That is the A camp: 10,11,12,15,16,18,3,4,6,7.

The B camp, 13,14,9, re-defines per-exposure efficacy conditionally on a responder: protected fraction has 100% per-exposure reduction, susceptible fraction has 0%. Then the marginal 1-IRR = p <100% and is described as an underestimate of the biological per-exposure effect in responders.

Current tension is definitional: population-average per-exposure VE = p vs responder-conditional per-exposure VE =100%. Under the standard population-average definition the rate ratio is biased upward for any realistic T>0, with the bias growing with follow-up and attack rate; the cumulative risk ratio 1-RR stays at p. I am leaning to the conventional teaching that 1-incidence rate ratio overestimates per-exposure efficacy for an all-or-nothing vaccine, with the caveat about definition of per-exposure VE. Unresolved is which definition the question intends; majority of detailed derivations support A overestimate.

The debate is about the definition of “per-exposure vaccine efficacy’’ and how the incidence-density estimator behaves under an all-or-nothing mechanism.

All-or-nothing model: fraction p completely protected, fraction 1-p fully susceptible, unvaccinated hazard λ0(t). 
S0(t)=exp[-Λ0(t)], Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t). 
Instantaneous vaccinated hazard
hV(t)= -d log Sv/dt = (1-p)h0(t)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)].
Hence instantaneous hazard ratio

EventsV(T)= (1-p)N[1-S0(T)],

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For a pure all-or-nothing vaccine with proportion p completely protected and 1-p phenotypically unvaccinated, let λ0 be the unvaccinated force of infection.

$S_u(t)=\exp[-\lambda_0 t]$,  $S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S_u(t)$

$h_v(t)=-\frac{d}{dt}\log S_v(t)=\lambda_0\frac{(1-p)S_u(t)}{p+(1-p)S_u(t)}$

$h_u(t)=\lambda_0$,

so the instantaneous hazard ratio is

$HR(t)=\frac{h_v(t)}{h_u(t)}=\frac{(1-p)S_u(t)}{p+(1-p)S_u(t)}\le 1-p$,

$HR(0)=1-p$, $HR(t)\downarrow0$ as $t\to\infty$.

The true per-exposure / per-contact reduction is the initial hazard ratio

$VE_{e}=1-HR(0)=p$,

and the cumulative risk ratio is constant

$F_v(T)=(1-p)[1-S_u(T)]$,   $RR(T)=1-p$,   $1-RR(T)=p$.

The incidence density that is used for 1-IRR is the time average,

$IR_v(T)=\frac{(1-p)[1-S_u(T)]}{pT+(1-p)\int_0^T S_u(s)ds}$,
$IR_u=\lambda_0$,

$IRR(T)=\frac{1-p}{p\lambda_0T/[1-S_u(T)]+(1-p)}<1-p$ for any $T>0$.

Hence

$1-IRR(T)=\frac{p\lambda_0T}{p\lambda_0T+(1-p)[1-S_u(T)]}>p$,

with $1-IRR(T)\to p$ as $T\to0$ and $1-IRR(T)\to1$ as $T\to\infty$.
The $p$ fraction that is never at risk contributes immortal, event free person-time to the vaccinated denominator, the susceptible $1-p$ fraction is progressively depleted by infection, so the average hazard in the vaccinated arm declines with follow-up.

The time-averaged $1-IRR$ is therefore an upwardly biased estimator of the proportion protected $p$, i.e. of the population-average per-exposure efficacy $1-HR(0)$. The unbiased estimator for the all-or-nothing proportion protected is the cumulative risk ratio $1-RR=p$. For a leaky vaccine $HR(t)$ is constant and $1-IRR=VE_e$.

The ‘correctly estimate’ and ‘underestimate’ readings follow from redefining per-exposure efficacy as the population-mean hazard reduction $\lambda_V/\lambda_0=1-p$, or as the $100\%$ biological effect conditional on being a responder. Under the conventional per-exposure definition $VE_e=1-HR(0)=p$, $1-IRR$ overestimates it for any realistic finite follow-up.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the confusion in this thread is mostly definitional, and once we make the definition explicit the direction becomes clearer.

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the per-exposure effect is binary at the individual level: a fraction p is completely removed from risk, i.e. 100% reduction in the probability of infection given an exposure, and the remaining fraction 1-p remains biologically identical to unvaccinated, i.e. 0% reduction per exposure in that stratum.

risk_v per exposure = p × 0 + (1-p) × risk_0 per exposure = (1-p) risk_0.

and

λ_u = λ_0
and

so 1-IRR = p.

I think the confusion here is really about which hazard we are talking about – the marginal population incidence density that goes into an IRR, versus the conditional hazard among those who remain at risk.

In an all-or-nothing model with fraction p completely protected and 1-p fully susceptible:

* Unvaccinated incidence density = λ0
* Vaccinated population average incidence density = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0 = (1-p)λ0

Under constant exposure intensity the incidence rate ratio is therefore

IRR = λV / λU = 1-p

and

1-IRR = p

That p is the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated cohort: average per-exposure risk vaccinated = (1-p) × risk per exposure unvaccinated. The per-exposure vaccine efficacy on the population average scale is 1 - average riskV / average riskU = p.

The time-dependent HR(t)= (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] that is quoted a lot is the hazard conditional on still being uninfected and therefore still contributing to the risk set. It declines because the 1-p susceptible fraction is progressively depleted by infection while the p protected fraction stays in the denominator. That is a conditional hazard, not the marginal incidence density that is actually used to compute an incidence rate ratio.

An IRR is events divided by total person-time accrued by the whole vaccinated cohort, protected person-time included. The protected person-time is not “immortal” in the sense of biasing the rate – it is the correct denominator for the average rate per vaccinated person, which is exactly the average per-exposure risk we want.

Hence on the usual epidemiologic population-average definition of per-exposure VE, the rate ratio is constant in time for an all-or-nothing vaccine and 1-IRR = p is the per-exposure efficacy. The cumulative risk ratio declines with follow-up, and the distinction between all-or-nothing and leaky shows up there, not in the marginal incidence rate ratio.

That is why colleagues 17, 2, 5 and 8 get 1-IRR = p as the population-average per-exposure VE. The “overestimate” argument mixes the conditional hazard given survival with the marginal incidence density used for IRR, and also conflates the biological 100% protection in the responder sub-cohort with the population average protection which by definition is p.

I think the confusion in this thread is mostly definitional, and once we make the definition explicit the direction becomes clearer.

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the per-exposure effect is binary at the individual level: a fraction p is completely removed from risk, i.e. 100% reduction in the probability of infection given an exposure, and the remaining fraction 1-p remains biologically identical to unvaccinated, i.e. 0% reduction per exposure in that stratum.

What 1-IRR gives us is the population-average reduction in incidence per unit person-time,

IRR = λV / λU = 1-p ,   1-IRR = p,

the proportion of vaccinees who are rendered non-susceptible. That is a population-average, mixture quantity. It is the average reduction in the rate of infection in the whole vaccinated cohort, averaged over the p never-at-risk person-time and the 1-p susceptible person-time.

Per-exposure vaccine efficacy is normally meant as the biological effect conditional on an exposure in a person who can still be infected, i.e. the reduction in Pr(infection|exposure) for a responder. In the protected sub-cohort that reduction is essentially 100%. The marginal 1-IRR = p < 1 is the average over responders and non-responders, and it is diluted down by the 1-p who contribute events at the unvaccinated rate.

In that responder-biological sense 1-IRR is a conservative, downward-biased summary of the per-exposure protection that is actually realized when the vaccine acts. The remark made by Colleague 1 captures it well: in responder-specific language 1-IRR is an underestimate of the 100% biological per-exposure effect, with p being the fraction of individuals who experience that 100% effect rather than the per-exposure reduction itself.

That is why the constant-hazard population-average derivation λV = p·0 + (1-p)λ0, i.e. IRR = 1-p, is correct for the average rate reduction, but it is not the conditional per-exposure efficacy for the susceptible sub-population. The depletion of susceptibles with follow-up that drives HR(t) down is depletion of the at-risk pool, not a change in per-exposure risk for those who remain susceptible. For that reason 1-IRR is best read as an underestimate of the true biological per-exposure protection, and as a population-average proportion protected.

$T>0$,

The $p$ fraction contributes event-free immortal person-time, inflating the denominator of the vaccinated rate and depleting the susceptible $1-p$ risk set by infection.

Therefore

$1-IRR(T)=\frac{p\lambda_{0}T}{p\lambda_{0}T+(1-p)[1-S_{u}(T)]}>p=1-HR(0)$,

and $1-IRR(T)$ increases monotonically with follow-up and attack rate toward $1$. The time-averaged incidence-rate based VE is $>p$ and is an upwardly biased proxy for the instantaneous per-exposure reduction $p=1-HR(0)$. In the limit of short follow-up it tends to $p$; with realistic follow-up it overestimates the population-average per-exposure efficacy. The unbiased estimator of the all-or-nothing proportion protected is the cumulative risk ratio, $1-RR_{cum}=p$, not the rate ratio.

That is the usual immortal person-time dilution and is the reason the rate ratio is constant $1-p$ only on the marginal hazard level $\lambda_{V}=(1-p)\lambda_{0}$ and not on the observable finite-follow-up incidence density.

I think the confusion here is really about which definition of “per-exposure” we are using, and the textbook population-average definition is the one that is normally meant by per-exposure vaccine efficacy in rate studies.

For an all-or-nothing vaccine with proportion p completely protected and 1-p phenotypically unvaccinated, with a constant exposure intensity the marginal per-exposure risk in the vaccinated population is

risk_v per exposure = p × 0 + (1-p) × risk_0 per exposure = (1-p) risk_0.

Hence the average per-exposure risk ratio is
RR_pe = (1-p) risk_0 / risk_0 = 1-p,
and
VE_pe = 1 - RR_pe = p.

Under constant exposure the incidence rate is exposure rate × per-exposure risk, so
λ_v = p·0 + (1-p) λ_0 = (1-p) λ_0,
λ_u = λ_0
and
IRR = λ_v / λ_u = 1-p,
so 1-IRR = p.

That is exactly the population average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated cohort. The cumulative risk ratio is the same,
R_v(T)/R_u(T) = [1-p][1-S_0(T)] / [1-S_0(T)] = 1-p,
so 1-RR(T)=p as well. In the population-average sense rate and risk track each other.

The HR(t) = (1-p) S_u(t) / [p + (1-p)S_u(t)] that is quoted for the overestimate argument is the hazard conditional on having survived to time t, i.e. the instantaneous force of infection among the still uninfected. It declines because the susceptible 1-p fraction is progressively depleted by infection while the p fraction remains. That is a selection effect in the risk set, not a change in the per-exposure risk for a person who remains susceptible. The susceptible vaccinated individuals who remain at risk continue to have the same per-exposure risk as unvaccinated persons, and the marginal population average per-exposure risk stays (1-p) times the unvaccinated risk for the whole follow-up.

The remark about “immortal person-time” is therefore a re-description of the fact that the protected fraction contributes zero events. That zero contribution is precisely how the average per-exposure risk is reduced to (1-p) risk_0. Counting their person-time is correct for a population-average rate, because the exposure rate per calendar time is unchanged and the average number of events per unit calendar time is reduced by the proportion protected.

If per-exposure efficacy is defined conditionally on a responder, i.e. biologically 100% in the p fraction, then 1-IRR = p is indeed an average over responders and non-responders. That is the usual population-average definition used for VE_IRR, and under that standard definition the incidence rate ratio correctly estimates the per-exposure vaccine efficacy, VE_pe = p, for an all-or-nothing mechanism, just as it does for a leaky mechanism.

I think the time-varying hazard derivation is correct and it is important to be precise about what we mean by “per-exposure”.

Formally with an all-or-nothing model

S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S_0(t),   h_v(t)=(1-p)λ0 S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]

so h_v(t)/h_0(t)= (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] < 1-p for t>0. The average incidence density over follow-up is therefore diluted by the event-free person-time contributed by the p fraction that is never at risk, and the marginal 1-IRR(T) = p λ0 T/[p λ0 T+(1-p)[1-S0(T)]] > p and increases with T. That is a statement about the population averaged hazard.

Per-exposure vaccine efficacy is the biological reduction in risk given an exposure in a susceptible individual, not the marginal reduction in the whole vaccinated cohort. In an all-or-nothing mechanism the vaccine does not attenuate risk per exposure in the 1-p susceptible fraction, it removes a fraction p of vaccinees from the risk set completely. Conditional on being a responder the per-exposure risk is zero, i.e. 100% protection per exposure, and conditional on being a non-responder the per-exposure risk is the same as unvaccinated, i.e. 0% protection per exposure.

The marginal incidence rate ratio 1-IRR = p is the population average of those two extremes: p×100% + (1-p)×0%. It is the fraction of individuals who are made immune, the average population reduction in incidence per person-time. It averages the complete block of exposure in responders with the full risk in non-responders. 

Hence relative to the biological per-exposure effect that is realized in the protected sub-cohort, the marginal 1-IRR is a diluted, conservative summary. It reports the proportion protected, not the 100% per-exposure reduction experienced when the vaccine does act. In that responder-specific, per-contact sense the incidence-rate based VE is downward-biased, i.e. it underestimates the true per-exposure protection conferred by the vaccine in those who respond. This is the same distinction Colleague 1 makes in the remark about responder-specific language, and it is why the rate ratio is often described as a population-average rather than a per-exposure biological efficacy for an all-or-nothing vaccine.

I think the population-average framing resolves the confusion that is driving the overestimate camp.

In an all-or-nothing model the vaccinated cohort is a mixture. A fraction p is made completely non-susceptible, hazard = 0, and a fraction 1-p is phenotypically identical to unvaccinated with hazard λ0(t). On a per person-time basis, and with the same exposure intensity in the two arms, the marginal hazard seen in the vaccinated arm is the mixture

λV(t) = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0(t) = (1-p) λ0(t)

so that

HR(t) = λV(t)/λ0(t) = 1-p

is constant in time. The incidence rate is exposure rate × per-exposure risk, and with constant exposure

IRV = (1-p) IRU

IRR = IRV/IRU = 1-p

and

VE_IR = 1-IRR = p

That p is exactly the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated population: the average per-exposure risk in vaccinated is p·0 + (1-p)·r0 = (1-p)r0, so the per-exposure risk ratio is 1-p and the per-exposure VE is 1-(1-p)=p.

The time-dependent conditional hazard

hV(t)= (1-p) λ0 Su(t)/[ p + (1-p) Su(t) ]

that colleagues 10,11,15,16,18 write down is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected up to time t. It declines because the 1-p susceptible fraction is progressively depleted by infection while the p protected fraction continues to contribute event-free person-time. That is a statement about the risk set enrichment over time and it makes the cumulative risk ratio 1-RR(t)=p decline in the usual sense, and it is why the cumulative risk ratio is not constant under all-or-nothing.

It does not make the marginal incidence density time-varying. The incidence density is total events / total person-time. Expected events in vaccinated = (1-p) × expected events in an equivalent unvaccinated cohort, and expected person-time contributed by the vaccinated cohort is the mixture of p person-time with zero events and (1-p) person-time with the same exposure as unvaccinated. The ratio therefore stays 1-p.

Hence on the usual population-average definition of per-exposure efficacy – the average reduction in the probability of infection per unit exposure across the vaccinated population – 1-IRR = p is the correct estimator. The distinction is between the population-average per-exposure effect, which is p, and the responder-specific conditional effect, which is 100% in the protected subgroup. The incidence rate ratio estimates the former without bias, which is the standard per-exposure VE used for all-or-nothing vaccines.

I’m with Colleagues 2,5,8 and 17 on the population-average reading of “per-exposure”.

In an all-or-nothing model a fraction p is made biologically non- susceptible and 1-p is left biologically identical to unvaccinated. Let r0 be the probability of infection given a single exposure in an unvaccinated susceptible person and let the exposure intensity be constant across individuals and arms. Then

E[ r | vaccinated ] = p·0 + (1-p)·r0 = (1-p) r0

so the average per-exposure risk ratio is

RR_pe = E[r|v]/r0 = 1-p

and the average per-exposure vaccine efficacy is

VE_pe = 1-RR_pe = p.

With constant exposure intensity the incidence rate is exposure rate × per-exposure risk, so on the marginal population level

λ_v = exposure·E[r|v] = exposure·(1-p) r0 = (1-p) λ_u

and

IRR = λ_v/λ_u = 1-p,   1-IRR = p.

That is exactly the proportion completely protected and it is the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated cohort. 

The time-declining conditional hazard h_v(t)/h_u(t) = (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] that Colleagues 10,11,15,16,18 derive is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected to time t. It declines because the 1-p susceptible fraction is being selectively depleted by infection while the p protected fraction remains in the risk set. That is a selection / enrichment phenomenon, not a change in the biological per-exposure susceptibility of an individual who remains susceptible. Conditional on being in the susceptible stratum the per-exposure risk stays r0, and conditional on being in the protected stratum it stays 0.

The “immortal person-time” inflation of the denominator therefore biases the cumulative risk ratio and the time-averaged hazard, i.e. it is why 1-RR(T) < p and why the calendar-time average hazard falls with follow-up. It does not change the average per-exposure risk per exposure under constant exposure intensity, which is what IRR is estimating. On the usual population-average definition of per-exposure efficacy the incidence rate ratio is constant and 1-IRR = p correctly recovers the average per-exposure reduction.

The distinction is the conditional vs marginal definition. If per-exposure efficacy were defined conditionally on the 1-p susceptible sub-cohort, the conditional VE is 0 for those individuals and 100% for the protected individuals. The marginal 1-IRR = p is the population average of that, and it is the quantity normally reported as VE per exposure for an all-or-nothing vaccine.

The all-or-nothing model is a mixture: fraction p completely protected, fraction 1-p fully susceptible with unvaccinated hazard λ0. 
S_u = exp(-λ0 t), S_v = p + (1-p)S_u
h_v(t)= λ0 (1-p)S_u /[p+(1-p)S_u], h_u=λ0
HR(t)= (1-p)S_u/[p+(1-p)S_u] ≤ 1-p, HR(0)=1-p, HR(t)→0. 
Cumulative risk F_v=(1-p)F_u so risk ratio RR(t)=1-p constant, 1-RR=p = proportion protected.

Incidence density over finite T: 
E_v=(1-p)[1-S_u], PT_v = pT+(1-p)∫S_u
IR_v = (1-p)[1-S_u]/[pT+(1-p)∫S_u], IR_u=λ0
IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-S_u]/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-S_u]] <1-p for T>0
1-IRR(T)= pλ0T/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-S_u]] > p, →p as T→0, →1 as T→∞.
The p fraction contributes event-free immortal person-time, the 1-p susceptible fraction is depleted by infection, so the time-averaged hazard < HR(0). Hence 1-IRR(T) is upwardly biased for the instantaneous per-exposure/proportion protected efficacy p=1-HR(0). Unbiased estimator for all-or-nothing is cumulative risk ratio 1-RR=p.

Definitional split remains:
* Population-average instantaneous / marginal mixture hazard: λV = p·0+(1-p)λ0 = (1-p)λ0, so marginal HR =1-p constant. With this definition VE_pop =1-IRR =p and the rate ratio is said to correctly estimate the average reduction in risk per exposure across the whole vaccinated cohort, and to be constant in time, unlike cumulative risk.
* Per-exposure/biological conditional definition: per-contact reduction for a responder is 100%, for a non-responder 0%. The marginal 1-IRR=p is the average of those extremes. In that responder-specific language 1-IRR is a diluted conservative summary and is described as an underestimate of the 100% biological effect realized in protected individuals.
* Finite-follow-up person-time definition: the usual epidemiologic 1-IRR computed from total cases/total person-time over realistic follow-up is >p, i.e. overestimates the per-exposure/proportion protected efficacy p, with bias growing with follow-up and attack rate. This is the classic “immortal person-time”/all-or-nothing dilution argument.

Majority in both rounds, colleagues 10,11,12,15,16,18,3,4,6,7,1, etc., argue overestimate A for realistic finite follow-up per-exposure VE =1-HR(0)=p.
Colleagues 1,2,5,8,14,17 argue correctly estimate C under the usual population-average definition λV/λU=1-p.
Colleagues 13,14,9 argue underestimate B if per-exposure efficacy is defined conditionally on a responder =100%.

Unresolved: the phrasing “per-exposure vaccine efficacy” is ambiguous between population-average instantaneous reduction p and responder-conditional 100% protection. The question as conventionally taught in vaccine epidemiology points to the finite-follow-up rate-ratio bias → overestimate A.

reflection_text.10:
The all-or-nothing model is p completely protected, 1-p fully susceptible with unvaccinated hazard λ0. Survival Sv(t)=p+(1-p)Su(t), Su=exp(-λ0t). Conditional hazard in vaccinated hv(t)=λ0(1-p)Su/[p+(1-p)Su]; hu=λ0. Hence instantaneous HR(t)=(1-p)Su/[p+(1-p)Su] ≤1-p, HR(0)=1-p, HR(t)→0 with time. Cumulative risk Fv=(1-p)F0 so cumulative risk ratio RRcum=1-p constant, 1-RRcum=p.

Population-average per-exposure risk = (1-p) risk0, so population-average VE per exposure = p =1-HR(0). That is the proportion protected.

Incidence density over finite T is events/PT. PTv = NpT +(1-p)N∫Su ds, eventsv = (1-p)N[1-Su(T)]. So IRv/IRu = (1-p)[1-Su]/[p λ0 T +(1-p)[1-Su]] = (1-p)/[p λ0 T/(1-Su)+(1-p)] <1-p for T>0. Hence average HR < HR(0). So 1-IRR(T)=p λ0 T/[p λ0 T+(1-p)[1-Su]] >p, increasing with T →1 as T→∞. Protected person-time is immortal/inflates denominator, depleting susceptible risk set.

Thus a time-averaged incidence-density based VE is upwardly biased relative to instantaneous per-exposure reduction p =1-HR(0). The bias grows with follow-up/attack rate. Cumulative risk ratio 1-RRcum=p is unbiased for proportion protected.

Current round disagreement mirrors previous:
- Overestimate camp: 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,4,6,7,3. They use hv(t) declining, time-averaged IRR <1-p, so 1-IRR >p > instantaneous per-exposure VE. Emphasise immortal person-time of p fraction dilutes IRv and makes 1-IRR an upwardly biased proxy for the proportion protected / initial HR. The limit T→0 recovers p; realistic T gives overestimate.
- Correctly-estimate camp: 2,5,8,14. Argue marginal population hazard λV = p·0+(1-p)λ0 = (1-p)λ0 constant, so IRR=1-p and 1-IRR=p is the population-average reduction in risk per exposure under constant exposure intensity. The declining conditional HR(t) is hazard given survival, a selection/enrichment effect, not a change in per-exposure susceptibility of remaining susceptibles. Under the usual epidemiologic population-average definition of per-exposure VE, 1-IRR correctly recovers p.
- Underestimate camp: 13,14,9,2 remark. Define per-exposure efficacy biologically conditional on being a responder: responder efficacy =100% per exposure, non-responder =0%. Marginal 1-IRR=p averages those extremes, so relative to the 100% biological effect in responders it is a diluted, conservative/underestimate summary.

Key unresolved definition: per-exposure VE = 1-HR(0)=p instantaneous/proportion protected vs population-average hazard reduction =p vs responder-specific biological 100%. Under the conventional finite follow-up incidence density interpretation taught for all-or-nothing vs leaky, 1-IRR overestimates the true per-exposure reduction p, with unbiased estimator being cumulative risk ratio 1-RR=p. If per-exposure is defined as population-average hazard reduction, 1-IRR = p is correct on average. The overestimate statement is the classic immortal person-time dilution argument.

HR(t)=h_v/h_u = (1-p)S_u(t)/[p+(1-p)S_u(t)] ≤ 1-p
HR(0)=1-p, HR(t)↓0.

The instantaneous per-exposure / proportion-protected efficacy is
VE_e=1-HR(0)=p and the cumulative risk ratio is constant
F_v(T)=(1-p)F_u(T) , RR_cum(T)=1-p , 1-RR_cum=p.

The incidence density used for IRR is events / total person-time.

PT_v(T)=NpT+(1-p)N∫0^T S_u(s)ds

person-time for the whole follow-up, inflating the vaccinated denominator
while the 1-p susceptible fraction is progressively depleted by infection.

1-IRR is an upwardly biased proxy for the instantaneous per-exposure

3.text:
A. overestimate

For a pure all-or-nothing mechanism with proportion $p$ completely protected and $1-p$ phenotypically unvaccinated, let the unvaccinated force of infection be $\lambda_{0}$.

$S_{u}(t)=e^{-\lambda_{0}t}$ , $S_{v}(t)=p+(1-p)S_{u}(t)$

$h_{v}(t)=-\frac{d}{dt}\log S_{v}(t)=\lambda_{0}\frac{(1-p)S_{u}(t)}{p+(1-p)S_{u}(t)}$, $h_{u}(t)=\lambda_{0}$

$HR(t)=\dfrac{h_{v}}{h_{u}}=\dfrac{(1-p)S_{u}(t)}{p+(1-p)S_{u}(t)}\le 1-p$

$HR(0)=1-p$, $HR(t)\downarrow0$ as $t\to\infty$.

Hence the instantaneous per-exposure / proportion protected efficacy is

$VE_{e}=1-HR(0)=p$ 

and the cumulative risk ratio is constant

$F_{v}(T)=(1-p)F_{u}(T)$ , $RR_{cum}(T)=1-p$, $1-RR_{cum}=p$.

The incidence density that is used in practice is cases per total person-time. With $N$ per arm

$E_{v}(T)=N(1-p)[1-S_{u}(T)]$,
$PT_{v}(T)=NpT+(1-p)N\int_{0}^{T}S_{u}(s)ds$,

$IR_{v}(T)=\dfrac{(1-p)[1-S_{u}(T)]}{pT+(1-p)\int_{0}^{T}S_{u}(s)ds}$,
$IR_{u}=\lambda_{0}$.

Hence for constant $\lambda_{0}$

$IRR(T)=\dfrac{IR_{v}}{IR_{u}}=
\frac{(1-p)[1-S_{u}(T)]}{p\lambda_{0}T+(1-p)[1-S_{u}(T)]}<1-p$, $T>0$,

$1-IRR(T)=\dfrac{p\lambda_{0}T}{p\lambda_{0}T+(1-p)[1-S_{u}(T)]}>p$,

$1-IRR(T)\to p$ as $T\to0$ and $1-IRR(T)\to1$ as $T\to\infty$.

The $p$ fraction contributes event-free, effectively immortal, person-time for the whole follow-up while the $1-p$ susceptible fraction is progressively depleted by infection. The time-averaged hazard is therefore $<HR(0)=1-p$, i.e. $\overline{HR}<HR(0)$. The conventional finite-follow-up cases-per-person-time $1-IRR$ is a person-time diluted average and is upwardly biased for the instantaneous per-exposure reduction $p=1-HR(0)$. The unbiased estimator of the all-or-nothing proportion protected is the cumulative risk ratio $1-RR_{cum}=p$.

The population-average instantaneous limit $\lim_{T\to0}1-IRR=p$ and the marginal mixture $\lambda_{V}=(1-p)\lambda_{0}$ give the statement that $1-IRR=p$ on the population-average hazard scale, and the responder-specific $100\%$ effect in the $p$ protected sub-cohort is diluted to $p$ on the marginal scale. Under the usual epidemiologic finite follow-up incidence density definition the rate-based VE overstates the per-exposure proportion-protected efficacy $p$, the bias growing with follow-up and attack rate. For a leaky vaccine $HR(t)$ is constant and $1-IRR=VE_{e}$.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

The disagreement in this thread is almost entirely definitional, and once the definition of “per-exposure” is made explicit the incidence rate ratio is doing exactly what it is supposed to do for an all-or-nothing mechanism.

Let r0 be the probability of infection given a single exposure in an unvaccinated susceptible person and let exposure intensity be constant across arms. In an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p is made biologically non-susceptible and 1-p is phenotypically identical to unvaccinated. The average per-exposure risk in the vaccinated cohort is therefore the mixture

E[r | v] = p·0 + (1-p)·r0 = (1-p) r0

so that on the population average scale

RR_pe = E[r|v] / r0 = 1-p
VE_pe = 1 - RR_pe = p

With constant exposure intensity incidence rate = exposure rate × per-exposure risk, so on the marginal population level

λ_v = exposure·E[r|v] = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0 = (1-p) λ0
λ_u = λ0

and

IRR = λ_v / λ_u = 1-p ,    1-IRR = p

That is the average reduction in risk per exposure across the vaccinated population, which is the standard epidemiologic meaning of per-exposure VE in rate studies.

The time declining conditional hazard

h_v(t)= λ0 (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)],   HR(t)= (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]

that is quoted for the overestimate argument is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected up to time t. It declines because the 1-p susceptible fraction is progressively depleted by infection while the p protected fraction continues to contribute event-free person-time. That is a risk-set enrichment / selection effect, not a change in the biological per-exposure susceptibility of individuals who remain susceptible. Conditional on being in the susceptible stratum the per-exposure risk stays r0, and conditional on being protected it stays 0.

Counting the person-time contributed by the p protected fraction is not “immortal person-time bias” for the marginal rate; it is the correct denominator for the average rate per vaccinated person. The protected person-time is precisely how the average events per calendar time are reduced by the proportion protected.

The cumulative risk ratio is the same, F_v(T)/F_u(T)=1-p, so 1-RR(T)=p.

The marginal 1-IRR = p is the population average of 100% protection in the p fraction and 0% in the 1-p fraction, which is exactly the average per-exposure efficacy the rate ratio is designed to estimate. On the population-average hazard scale the quantity $1-HR(0)=p$ is the average reduction in hazard per person-time, i.e. the fraction of the cohort made immune. Biologically, per-exposure efficacy is the reduction in $\Pr(\text{infection}\mid\text{exposure})$ for a host in whom the vaccine can act. In an all-or-nothing mechanism that reduction is binary: conditional on being a responder the vaccine gives essentially 100% protection per exposure, conditional on being a non-responder it gives 0% protection per exposure. $IRR = \lambda_V/\lambda_U =1-p$

is the mixture $p\times0 + (1-p)\times1$ of those two biological states. It is the population-average proportion protected, not the biological per-exposure effect realized when the vaccine does act.

As Colleague 1 notes in his own remark, in responder-specific language $1-IRR$ is an underestimate of the 100% biological per-exposure effect, with $p$ being the fraction of individuals who experience that 100% effect rather than the per-exposure reduction itself.

That is the same point Colleague 13 and Colleague 2 make: the declining conditional hazard $h_v(t)$ is depletion of the at-risk pool, not a change in per-exposure risk for those who remain susceptible. The per-exposure risk for a susceptible vaccinated person stays $r_0$, for a protected responder it stays $0$. The marginal $1-IRR$ is a conservative, population-averaged summary of that 100% biological block and therefore underestimates the true per-exposure protection conferred by the vaccine in those who respond.

* non-responder, fraction 1-p: per-exposure risk =r0, per-exposure VE =0%

The marginal incidence density that enters an IRR is
λv = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0 = (1-p)λu
so that IRR =1-p and 1-IRR =p.

1-IRR =p is therefore the population-average of the two extremes, p×100% + (1-p)×0%. It is the average reduction in incidence per person-time and the proportion of vaccinees who are rendered immune. It is not the biological per-exposure reduction realized when the vaccine does act.

In responder-specific, per-contact language the vaccine confers essentially complete block of infection when it works. The marginal 1-IRR averages that 100% biological block with the 0% effect in the 1-p phenotypically unvaccinated fraction and is diluted down to the proportion protected p. Relative to the 100% per-exposure protection experienced in responders, the population-average 1-IRR is a conservative, downward-biased summary of the true per-exposure efficacy.

That is the distinction Colleague 1 notes in the remark about responder-specific language: on a conditional biological per-exposure definition the 1-IRR is an underestimate of the 100% effect in the protected sub-cohort, with p being the fraction of individuals who experience that effect rather than the per-exposure reduction itself. The time-varying HR(t) is risk-set enrichment, not a change in per-exposure risk for those who remain susceptible.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

The rate ratio that is actually used in practice is the marginal incidence density for the whole vaccinated cohort, not the conditional hazard among those who remain uninfected.

In an all-or-nothing model the vaccinated population is a mixture
p with hazard 0 and 1-p with hazard λ0(t). With constant exposure intensity

E[risk per exposure | vaccinated] = p·0 + (1-p)·r0 = (1-p)r0

so the average per-exposure risk ratio is 1-p and the average per-exposure VE is

VE_pe = 1 - (1-p) = p.

Under constant exposure the marginal incidence density is exposure rate × average per-exposure risk, hence

λV(t) = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0(t) = (1-p)λ0(t)

and

IRR = λV/λU = 1-p ,   1-IRR = p

is constant in time. That is the population-average reduction in risk per exposure across the vaccinated cohort, which is the standard epidemiologic definition of per-exposure VE.

The expression

hV(t)= λ0 (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]

that is repeatedly quoted is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected up to time t. It declines because the 1-p susceptible stratum is progressively depleted by infection while the p protected stratum stays in the risk set and continues to contribute event-free person-time. That is risk-set enrichment / selection, not a change in the biological per-exposure susceptibility of an individual who remains susceptible. Conditional on being susceptible the per-exposure risk stays r0, conditional on being protected it stays 0.

Counting the person-time of the p protected fraction in the denominator of the incidence rate is not immortal-person-time bias, it is the correct denominator for the average rate per vaccinated person. The protected person-time is exactly how the average per-exposure risk is reduced to (1-p)r0. The decline of the conditional hazard and the time-average of hV(t) is why the cumulative risk-based estimator is also 1-RR(T)=p, and it is why the marginal rate and the marginal cumulative risk are coherent.

The 100% biological effect in the responder sub-cohort is a conditional responder-specific effect. The marginal 1-IRR=p is the population average of 100% in the p fraction and 0% in the 1-p fraction, i.e. the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated population. On that conventional population-average definition the incidence rate ratio estimates per-exposure VE without bias for an all-or-nothing vaccine, just as it does for a leaky vaccine. The overestimate claim mixes the conditional hazard given survival with the marginal incidence density that IRR targets.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C correctly estimate

The confusion is between the marginal incidence density that defines an IRR and the conditional hazard among those who remain uninfected.

In an all-or-nothing model with fraction p completely protected and 1-p phenotypically identical to unvaccinated, with constant exposure intensity and constant per-exposure risk r0 in susceptibles:

E[ r | vaccinated ] = p·0 + (1-p)·r0 = (1-p) r0

Hence on the population-average scale

RR_pe = E[r|v]/r0 = 1-p
VE_pe = 1-RR_pe = p

With constant exposure intensity, incidence rate = exposure rate × per-exposure risk, so on the marginal population level

λV = p·0 + (1-p) λ0 = (1-p) λ0
λU = λ0

IRR = λV/λU = 1-p
1-IRR = p

That p is the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated cohort, which is the usual epidemiologic definition of per-exposure vaccine efficacy.

Sv(t)=p+(1-p)Su(t) and

hV(t)= -d log Sv/dt = λ0 (1-p)Su(t)/[p+(1-p)Su(t)]

is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected up to t. It declines because the 1-p susceptible fraction is progressively depleted by infection while the p protected fraction remains in the denominator. That is a risk-set enrichment / selection effect, not a change in the biological per-exposure susceptibility of an individual who remains susceptible. Conditional on being in the susceptible stratum the per-exposure risk stays r0, and conditional on being protected it stays 0.

An incidence rate ratio is total events divided by total person-time accrued by the whole vaccinated cohort, protected person-time included. The protected person-time is not a bias; it is the correct denominator for the average rate per vaccinated person, which is exactly the average per-exposure risk we want. Expected events in vaccinated = (1-p) × expected events in an equivalent unvaccinated cohort, and expected person-time is the mixture of p person-time with zero events and (1-p) person-time with the same exposure as unvaccinated. The ratio therefore stays 1-p.

The “immortal person-time” language describes why the cumulative risk ratio and the time-averaged conditional hazard fall with follow-up, i.e. why 1-RR(T) < p and why the calendar-time average hazard declines. It does not change the marginal average per-exposure risk per exposure under constant exposure intensity, which is what IRR estimates. On the standard population-average definition of per-exposure VE the incidence rate ratio is constant in time for an all-or-nothing vaccine and 1-IRR = p correctly recovers the average per-exposure reduction. The responder-specific 100% effect in the p sub-cohort is averaged to p on the population scale, which is the quantity normally reported as VE_IRR.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the disagreement is now really about what we mean by “per-exposure” and about marginal versus conditional hazard, not about the algebra.

The algebra everyone is writing down is correct. With p completely protected and 1-p phenotypically unvaccinated

S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S_0(t),   h_v(t)=λ0 (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)],   h_u(t)=λ0

so the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected up to time t,

HR_cond(t)=h_v(t)/h_u(t)=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]≤1-p,

declines from HR_cond(0)=1-p to 0. That is the hazard in the still-at-risk risk set. It declines because the 1-p susceptible fraction is selectively depleted by infection while the p protected fraction stays in the denominator. That is a selection/enrichment phenomenon in the risk set, not a change in the biological per-exposure risk of an individual who remains susceptible.

The incidence rate ratio that is used in practice is a marginal population quantity: total events divided by total person-time accrued by the whole vaccinated cohort, protected person-time included. On a per person-time basis the vaccinated cohort is a mixture

λ_V = p·0 + (1-p)·λ_0 = (1-p)λ_0

with the same exposure intensity in the two arms. Hence with constant exposure

IR_V = exposure × E[r|v] = exposure ×[p·0+(1-p)r_0] = (1-p)IR_U

and

IRR = IR_V/IR_U =1-p,   1-IRR =p.

That p is the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated population: average per-exposure risk vaccinated = (1-p) × risk per exposure unvaccinated, so the average per-exposure risk ratio is 1-p and the average per-exposure VE is 1-(1-p)=p.

The declining conditional HR(t) is exactly why the cumulative risk ratio stays constant, F_v(T)=(1-p)F_0(T), RR_cum(T)=1-p, 1-RR_cum=p. The “immortal person-time” that the A camp points to is the p person-time with zero events. Counting it is not a bias for a population-average rate; it is the correct denominator for the average rate per vaccinated person, i.e. the average per-exposure risk averaged over responders and non-responders.

In other words, 1-HR(0)=p is the population-average instantaneous per-exposure reduction at time zero, and under constant exposure the marginal incidence density ratio recovers that same p. The time-averaged 1-IRR is >p only if we redefine per-exposure VE as the instantaneous conditional hazard among survivors, 1-HR(t), and then compare it to a finite-follow-up average hazard. With the conventional epidemiologic definition of per-exposure VE as the average reduction in probability of infection per unit exposure across the vaccinated population, the rate ratio is constant and 1-IRR = p correctly estimates the population-average per-exposure efficacy. The responder-specific 100% protection is a conditional biological effect in the p sub-cohort; the marginal 1-IRR = p is the population average of that effect, which is the quantity normally reported as VE_IRR for an all-or-nothing vaccine.

IRR = λ_v / λ_u = 1-p ,    1-IRR = p
